igcse-0580-ordering-signed-values.description: Read signed values on a number line and decide when comparison signs include equality.

sections.title: What makes one signed value larger?
sections.label: Using the number line
sections.intro: Choose one fixed direction before comparing. A value increases as you move to the right, even while you are left of zero.

blocks.html: Place the numbers on the same scale. A number to the left is smaller. Between two negative numbers, the one further from zero is further left.

figure.alt: The point negative six sits left of negative two on a signed number line.
figure.caption: Moving right from \(-6\) to \(-2\) increases the value.

blocks.title: Compare signed whole numbers
blocks.hint: Decide which point is further left. Its value is smaller.
blocks.solution:
Start at zero. Both values lie on its left because they are negative.

The point at \(-7\) is further left than \(-3\).

Reading the pair in the requested order gives \(-3>-7\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. Reading the pair in the requested order gives \(-3>-7\).

blocks.html: The digit 7 is greater than 2, but the point −7 is further left than the point −2.

blocks.title: Compare negative decimals
blocks.hint: Compare the distances from zero, then check which negative number is further left.
blocks.solution:
The minus signs place both points left of zero. Use the larger distance from zero to find the point further left.

The distances are \(0.22\) and \(0.27\). The larger distance is \(0.27\).

\(-0.27\) is further left, so \(-0.22>-0.27\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. \(-0.27\) is further left, so \(-0.22>-0.27\).

blocks.html: Copy the relation in the order the question gives. If you swap the numbers, reverse the strict sign.

sections.title: Which signs make a comparison true?
sections.label: Strict, equal and inclusive signs
sections.intro: First decide whether the left value is smaller, equal or larger. Then read the requested sign from left to right.

blocks.html: The signs \(<\), \(=\) and \(>\) give three distinct comparisons. \(\ne\) is true for unequal values. \(\le\) or \(\ge\) may include the equal case.

blocks.title: Find all true symbols
blocks.prompt: Which option lists every symbol that makes \(4\;\square\;2\) true?
blocks.hint: Test the strict relation, then test equality and both inclusive signs.
blocks.solution:
The exact comparison is \(4>2\).

The left value is larger, so it is also at least the right value and the values differ.

The complete set of true symbols is \(>,\ \ge,\ \ne\).

retry.feedback: If two values are equal, the not-equal sign is false. Test each sign separately.

blocks.html: Two equal values can satisfy both inclusive comparisons. ‘More than’ excludes equality, and ‘at least’ includes it.

blocks.title: Include the boundary in ‘at most’
blocks.prompt: The temperature in a test chamber must be at most \(-2{}^\circ\mathrm C\). From the readings \(0,\quad -4,\quad -2,\quad -1,\quad -6\), select all the readings that meet the limit. Give their numerical values as a set.
blocks.hint: Include a reading that is exactly at the maximum allowed value.
blocks.solution:
At most means \(\le\). The chamber reading may equal its limit.

\(-6\) and \(-4\) are left of the limit. The reading \(-2\) is exactly at it.

The permitted readings are \(\left\{-6,-4,-2\right\}\).

field.label: All readings meeting the temperature limit

retry.feedback: ‘At most’ includes the reading equal to the limit.

blocks.html: Check whether the instruction asks for one sign from a list or all signs that make the comparison true.

sections.title: How do I apply a limit or order a whole list?
sections.label: Boundary words and ordering
sections.intro: Identify the comparison required by the wording. Sort left to right for smallest first, and right to left for largest first.

blocks.html: Use \(x\le b\) for ‘at most \(b\)’ and \(x\ge b\) for ‘at least \(b\)’. The strict forms exclude the boundary.

blocks.title: Distinguish ‘more than’ from ‘at least’
blocks.prompt: A label says that a carton contains more than 7 items. The possible counts are \(7,\quad 9,\quad 4,\quad 11,\quad 6\). Give all the counts that agree with the label as a set.
blocks.hint: Decide whether the wording includes equality before choosing the values.
blocks.solution:
‘More than 7’ means \(n>7\). It excludes \(7\).

Find the supplied points that lie to the right of this boundary.

The possible counts are \(\left\{9,11\right\}\).

field.label: Counts greater than the stated amount

retry.feedback: ‘More than’ is strict. Remove the value equal to the boundary.

blocks.html: Include a value equal to the limit only when the sign is inclusive.

blocks.title: Order a signed list
blocks.prompt: Write these values in order from smallest to largest. Fill the four positions in your answer: \(0,\quad -4,\quad 3,\quad -8\).
blocks.hint: Begin with the value furthest left. Include zero as its own entry.
blocks.solution:
All negative values are smaller than \(0\), so they go first.

\(-8\) lies left of \(-4\); place it first.

The full order is \(-8<-4<0<3\).

blocks.html: Before writing your last line, check the direction of the requested order and count every item.

examples.title: Compare signed whole numbers
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(-5\;\square\;-2\).
solution: Start at zero. Both values lie on its left because they are negative.
The point at \(-5\) is further left than \(-2\).
Reading the pair in the requested order gives \(-5<-2\).

examples.title: Compare negative decimals
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(-0.17\;\square\;-0.12\).
solution: The minus signs place both points left of zero. Use the larger distance from zero to find the point further left.
The distances are \(0.17\) and \(0.12\). The larger distance is \(0.17\).

examples.title: Find all true symbols
examples.question:
Which option lists every symbol that makes \(3\;\square\;3\) true?

A. \(<,\ \le,\ e\)   B. \(=,\ \le,\ \ge\)   C. \(>,\ \ge,\ e\)   D. \(=,\ e\)
solution: The exact comparison is \(3=3\).
Equal values satisfy both inclusive comparisons.
The complete set of true symbols is \(=,\ \le,\ \ge\).

examples.title: Include the boundary in ‘at most’
examples.question: The temperature in a test chamber must be at most \(-1{}^\circ\mathrm C\). From the readings \(1,\quad -3,\quad -1,\quad 0,\quad -5\), select all the readings that meet the limit. Give their numerical values as a set.
solution: At most means \(\le\). The chamber reading may equal its limit.
\(-5\) and \(-3\) are left of the limit. The reading \(-1\) is exactly at it.
The permitted readings are \(\left\{-5,-3,-1\right\}\).

examples.title: Distinguish ‘more than’ from ‘at least’
examples.question: A label says that a carton contains more than 6 items. The possible counts are \(6,\quad 8,\quad 3,\quad 10,\quad 5\). Give all the counts that agree with the label as a set.
solution: ‘More than 6’ means \(n>6\). It excludes \(6\).
Find the supplied points that lie to the right of this boundary.
The possible counts are \(\left\{8,10\right\}\).

examples.title: Order a signed list
examples.question: Write these values in order from smallest to largest. Fill the four positions in your answer: \(-7,\quad 2,\quad -3,\quad 0\).
solution: All negative values are smaller than \(0\), so they go first.
\(-7\) lies left of \(-3\); place it first.
The full order is \(-7<-3<0<2\).

The exact comparison is \(3<5\).

The left value is smaller, so it is also at most the right value and the values differ.

extraPractice.prompt: The temperature in a test chamber must be at most \(-3{}^\circ\mathrm C\). From the readings \(-1,\quad -5,\quad -3,\quad -2,\quad -7\), select all the readings that meet the limit. Give their numerical values as a set.

extraPractice.title: Distinguish ‘more than’ from ‘at least’
extraPractice.prompt: A label says that a carton contains more than 8 items. The possible counts are \(8,\quad 10,\quad 5,\quad 12,\quad 7\). Give all the counts that agree with the label as a set.
extraPractice.hint: Decide whether the wording includes equality before choosing the values.
extraPractice.solution:
‘More than 8’ means \(n>8\). It excludes \(8\).

Find the supplied points that lie to the right of this boundary.

The possible counts are \(\left\{10,12\right\}\).

field.label: Counts greater than the stated amount

retry.feedback: ‘More than’ is strict. Remove the value equal to the boundary.

extraPractice.title: Order a signed list
extraPractice.prompt: Write these values in order from smallest to largest. Fill the four positions in your answer: \(-9,\quad 4,\quad -5,\quad 0\).
extraPractice.hint: Begin with the value furthest left. Include zero as its own entry.

All negative values are smaller than \(0\), so they go first.

\(-9\) lies left of \(-5\); place it first.

The full order is \(-9<-5<0<4\).

glossary.definition: Uses a sign to show whether a non-zero quantity is positive or negative.
Uses \(<\) or \(>\) and excludes an equal value.
Uses \(\le\) or \(\ge\) and allows an equal value.
Starts with the smallest value and moves towards the largest.
Starts with the largest value and moves towards the smallest.

revision.body:
Using the number line

Place the numbers on the same scale. A number to the left is smaller. Between two negative numbers, the one further from zero is further left.

Strict, equal and inclusive signs

The signs \(<\), \(=\) and \(>\) give three distinct comparisons. \(\ne\) is true for unequal values. \(\le\) or \(\ge\) may include the equal case.

Boundary words and ordering

Use \(x\le b\) for ‘at most \(b\)’ and \(x\ge b\) for ‘at least \(b\)’. The strict forms exclude the boundary.

Example

\(-6<-2<0<3\)

Check yourself

  • What changes if ‘at least’ is replaced by ‘more than’?
  • Which is further right, \(-0.9\) or \(-0.86\)?

Answers The boundary is excluded. \(-0.86\) is further right.
revision.checks:
• The digit 7 is greater than 2, but the point −7 is further left than the point −2.
  • Two equal values can satisfy both inclusive comparisons. ‘More than’ excludes equality, and ‘at least’ includes it.
  • Include a value equal to the limit only when the sign is inclusive.
revision.examTip: Before writing your last line, check the direction of the requested order and count every item.

igcse-0580-ordering-same-form.description: Compare place-value columns, use equal-sized parts and make units match.

sections.title: Which decimal digit decides the order?
sections.label: Decimal columns
sections.intro: Compare from the largest place. Look at the first column where the digits differ.

blocks.html: Extend a decimal with trailing zeroes to make the columns easier to read. For example, \(0.47=0.470\) and \(0.437<0.470\).

figure.alt: A decimal line marks 0.437 and 0.47 in their correct places.
figure.caption: The point at \(0.437\) is to the left of \(0.47\).

blocks.title: Compare decimals digit by digit
blocks.hint: Write both numbers to thousandths without changing their values.
blocks.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Extend the shorter decimal with zeroes to show the same place-value columns.

Compare \(1.309\) and \(1.400\) from the left. The first differing column is the tenths column.

The comparison is \(1.309<1.4\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. The comparison is \(1.309<1.4\).

blocks.html: A decimal with more written digits can be the smaller value. Use the place of each digit.

blocks.title: Recognise equal decimals
blocks.hint: Check whether the extra digits change the value or only its written form.
blocks.solution:
The extra digits are zeroes after the last non-zero decimal digit.

These zeroes add zero thousandths and zero ten-thousandths. Both decimals are the same distance from zero.

The comparison is \(1.17=1.1700\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. The comparison is \(1.17=1.1700\).

blocks.html: Align decimal points in your working so the decisive column is visible.

sections.title: When can I compare the numerators?
sections.label: Fraction sizes
sections.intro: A numerator counts pieces. For it to decide which value is larger, each piece must have the same size.

blocks.html: Use a positive common denominator. Multiply the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same factor. If one fraction is above halfway and the other is below, use that benchmark.

blocks.title: Compare fractions using equal-sized parts
blocks.hint: Make the pieces the same size before counting them.
blocks.solution:
Make the fraction parts the same size. Use the positive common denominator 70.

\(\frac{6}{10}=\frac{42}{70}\) and \(\frac{8}{14}=\frac{40}{70}\).

Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{6}{10}>\frac{8}{14}\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{6}{10}>\frac{8}{14}\).

blocks.html: A larger denominator can mean smaller pieces. Comparing just the two denominators does not work in general.

blocks.title: Use one half as a benchmark
blocks.prompt: Which fraction in \(\frac{12}{20},\quad \frac{9}{20},\quad \frac{1}{2}\) is greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\)? Give the fraction.
blocks.hint: A fraction is greater than one half when its numerator is greater than half its positive denominator.
blocks.solution:
In 20 equal parts, halfway is 10 parts. The fraction \(\frac{9}{20}\) is below halfway.

12 parts is above halfway, so the fraction is \(\frac{12}{20}\).

The fraction \(\frac{1}{2}\) lies exactly at the halfway mark.

retry.feedback: The question says greater than. The half itself is the boundary.

blocks.html: Make both equivalent fractions visible in a non-calculator comparison.

sections.title: How do I compare measurements fairly?
sections.label: Common units and close values
sections.intro: Compare like quantities on the same scale. Decide which unit will make the comparison exact and convenient.

blocks.html: For centimetres and millimetres use \(1\,\mathrm{cm}=10\,\mathrm{mm}\). For a decimals-only list, keep the decimal forms and compare place-value columns.

blocks.title: Compare lengths in the same unit
blocks.hint: Compare the values after converting both to millimetres.
blocks.solution:
These are both lengths. Put them in the same unit before comparing.

Each centimetre has 10 millimetres, so \(3.4\,\mathrm{cm}=34\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Compare 34 mm and 34 mm. This gives \(3.4\,\mathrm{cm}=34\,\mathrm{mm}\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. Compare 34 mm and 34 mm. This gives \(3.4\,\mathrm{cm}=34\,\mathrm{mm}\).

blocks.html: Comparing the written numbers alone can reverse the order when units differ.

blocks.title: Order close decimals largest first
blocks.prompt: Write these values in order from largest to smallest: \(1.47,\quad 1.419,\quad 1.417\). Fill all three positions.
blocks.hint: Check the direction in the question and compare equally long decimal columns.
blocks.solution:
With three decimal places the values are \(1.417,\quad 1.470,\quad 1.419\).

Compare each column from left to right. Stop at the first differing digit.

Largest first gives \(1.470>1.419>1.417\).

blocks.html: Write the common unit next to your working and use the original measurements in your answer.

examples.title: Compare decimals digit by digit
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(1.3\;\square\;1.207\).
solution: Line up the decimal points. Extend the shorter decimal with zeroes to show the same place-value columns.
Compare \(1.300\) and \(1.207\) from the left. The first differing column is the tenths column.
The comparison is \(1.3>1.207\).

examples.title: Recognise equal decimals
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(1.1000\;\square\;1.10\).
solution: The extra digits are zeroes after the last non-zero decimal digit.
These zeroes add zero thousandths and zero ten-thousandths. Both decimals are the same distance from zero.
The comparison is \(1.1000=1.10\).

examples.title: Compare fractions using equal-sized parts
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(\frac{7}{12}\;\square\;\frac{4}{9}\).
solution: Make the fraction parts the same size. Use the positive common denominator 36.
Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{7}{12}>\frac{4}{9}\).

examples.title: Use one half as a benchmark
examples.question: Which fraction in \(\frac{6}{14},\quad \frac{1}{2},\quad \frac{9}{14}\) is greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\)? Give the fraction.
solution: In 14 equal parts, halfway is 7 parts. The fraction \(\frac{6}{14}\) is below halfway.
9 parts is above halfway, so the fraction is \(\frac{9}{14}\).
The fraction \(\frac{1}{2}\) lies exactly at the halfway mark.

examples.title: Compare lengths in the same unit
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}\;\square\;35\,\mathrm{mm}\).
solution: These are both lengths. Put them in the same unit before comparing.
Each centimetre has 10 millimetres, so \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}=31\,\mathrm{mm}\).
Compare 31 mm and 35 mm. This gives \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}<35\,\mathrm{mm}\).

examples.title: Order close decimals largest first
examples.question: Write these values in order from largest to smallest: \(1.017,\quad 1.07,\quad 1.019\). Fill all three positions.
solution: With three decimal places the values are \(1.017,\quad 1.070,\quad 1.019\).
Compare each column from left to right. Stop at the first differing digit.
Largest first gives \(1.070>1.019>1.017\).

extraPractice.title: Compare decimals digit by digit
extraPractice.hint: Write both numbers to thousandths without changing their values.
extraPractice.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Extend the shorter decimal with zeroes to show the same place-value columns.

Compare \(1.500\) and \(1.411\) from the left. The first differing column is the tenths column.

The comparison is \(1.5>1.411\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. The comparison is \(1.5>1.411\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise equal decimals
extraPractice.hint: Check whether the extra digits change the value or only its written form.
extraPractice.solution:
The extra digits are zeroes after the last non-zero decimal digit.

These zeroes add zero thousandths and zero ten-thousandths. Both decimals are the same distance from zero.

The comparison is \(1.2400=1.24\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. The comparison is \(1.2400=1.24\).

extraPractice.title: Compare fractions using equal-sized parts
extraPractice.hint: Make the pieces the same size before counting them.
extraPractice.solution:
Make the fraction parts the same size. Use the positive common denominator 176.

\(\frac{9}{16}=\frac{99}{176}\) and \(\frac{7}{11}=\frac{112}{176}\).

Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{9}{16}<\frac{7}{11}\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{9}{16}<\frac{7}{11}\).

extraPractice.title: Use one half as a benchmark
extraPractice.prompt: Which fraction in \(\frac{12}{26},\quad \frac{1}{2},\quad \frac{15}{26}\) is greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\)? Give the fraction.
extraPractice.hint: A fraction is greater than one half when its numerator is greater than half its positive denominator.
extraPractice.solution:
In 26 equal parts, halfway is 13 parts. The fraction \(\frac{12}{26}\) is below halfway.

15 parts is above halfway, so the fraction is \(\frac{15}{26}\).

The fraction \(\frac{1}{2}\) lies exactly at the halfway mark.

retry.feedback: The question says greater than. The half itself is the boundary.

extraPractice.title: Compare lengths in the same unit
extraPractice.hint: Compare the values after converting both to millimetres.
extraPractice.solution:
These are both lengths. Put them in the same unit before comparing.

Each centimetre has 10 millimetres, so \(3.7\,\mathrm{cm}=37\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Compare 37 mm and 31 mm. This gives \(3.7\,\mathrm{cm}>31\,\mathrm{mm}\).

retry.feedback: Read the sign from left to right. Compare 37 mm and 31 mm. This gives \(3.7\,\mathrm{cm}>31\,\mathrm{mm}\).

extraPractice.title: Order close decimals largest first
extraPractice.prompt: Write these values in order from largest to smallest: \(1.817,\quad 1.87,\quad 1.819\). Fill all three positions.
extraPractice.hint: Check the direction in the question and compare equally long decimal columns.
extraPractice.solution:
With three decimal places the values are \(1.817,\quad 1.870,\quad 1.819\).

Compare each column from left to right. Stop at the first differing digit.

Largest first gives \(1.870>1.819>1.817\).

glossary.definition: The value represented by a digit depends on its position.
A zero at the end of a decimal. It does not change the value.
A denominator shared by equivalent forms of the fractions.
An exact reference value such as one half.
The same unit used for every measurement being compared.

revision.body:
Decimal columns

Extend a decimal with trailing zeroes to make the columns easier to read. For example, \(0.47=0.470\) and \(0.437<0.470\).

Fraction sizes

Use a positive common denominator. Multiply the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same factor. If one fraction is above halfway and the other is below, use that benchmark.

Common units and close values

For centimetres and millimetres use \(1\,\mathrm{cm}=10\,\mathrm{mm}\). For a decimals-only list, keep the decimal forms and compare place-value columns.

Example

\(\frac{7}{12}=\frac{21}{36}>\frac{20}{36}=\frac{5}{9}\)

Check yourself

  • Which is greater, \(0.48\) or \(0.477\)?
  • Compare \(6.2\,\mathrm{cm}\) with \(64\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Answers \(0.48>0.477\). \(6.2\,\mathrm{cm}=62\,\mathrm{mm}<64\,\mathrm{mm}\).
revision.checks:
• A decimal with more written digits can be the smaller value. Use the place of each digit.
  • A larger denominator can mean smaller pieces. Comparing just the two denominators does not work in general.
  • Comparing the written numbers alone can reverse the order when units differ.
revision.examTip: Write the common unit next to your working and use the original measurements in your answer.

igcse-0580-ordering-mixed-forms.description: Find an exact comparison scale, retain ties and write final answers in their original forms.

sections.title: How can different forms share one scale?
sections.label: Exact equivalent values
sections.intro: Decide on a shared scale before sorting. Equivalent forms name the same point on the number line.

blocks.html: If all values give exact terminating decimals, use decimals for the working. A tie stays a tie when the forms change. Write an equals sign where two original values match.

figure.alt: A common number line locates 60 percent at 0.60 alongside 0.67 and 0.75.
figure.caption: Different labels such as \(60\%\) and \(\frac35\) sit at \(0.60\).

blocks.title: Order fractions, decimals and percentages
blocks.prompt: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(\frac{5}{20},\quad 28\%,\quad 0.259\). Enter the three values in the stated order.
blocks.hint: Make each number a decimal without rounding. The final positions keep both copies if two values are equal.
blocks.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(\frac{5}{20}=0.250\), \(28\%=0.280\), \(0.259\).

Compare digits from the left after aligning decimal points.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(\frac{5}{20}<0.259<28\%\).

blocks.html: Keep every original entry. Equal numbers can sit next to each other in either order when the list shows equality.

blocks.title: Keep an equality in the ordered list
blocks.prompt: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(\frac{5}{20},\quad 25\%,\quad 0.259\). Include both equal values and give the value of the tie.
blocks.hint: Make each number a decimal without rounding. The final positions keep both copies if two values are equal.
blocks.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(\frac{5}{20}=0.250\), \(25\%=0.250\), \(0.259\).

Compare digits from the left after aligning decimal points.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(\frac{5}{20}=25\%<0.259\).

fields.label: Value shared by the equal pair

blocks.html: Show your comparison scale, then return to the original fractions, decimals and percentages.

sections.title: What changes above one or below zero?
sections.label: Mixed numbers and negatives
sections.intro: A mixed number combines a whole part and a fraction. A negative sign moves a value to the negative side of the scale.

blocks.html: Retain the whole part when rewriting a positive mixed number. Compare signed values by position, and check the requested direction before writing your answer.

blocks.title: Order values above one
blocks.prompt: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(1\frac{2}{20},\quad 112\%,\quad 1.095\). Enter the three values in the stated order.
blocks.hint: Make each number a decimal without rounding. The final positions keep both copies if two values are equal.
blocks.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(1\frac{2}{20}=1.100\), \(112\%=1.120\), \(1.095\).

Compare digits from the left after aligning decimal points.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(1.095<1\frac{2}{20}<112\%\).

blocks.html: A percent above 100% is greater than one. A minus sign changes the position, not just the label.

blocks.title: Order negative values in different forms
blocks.prompt: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(-\frac{10}{20},\quad -52\%,\quad -0.495\). Enter the three values in the stated order.
blocks.hint: Make each number a decimal without rounding. The final positions keep both copies if two values are equal.
blocks.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(-\frac{10}{20}=-0.500\), \(-52\%=-0.520\), \(-0.495\).

All three values are negative. The one with the larger distance from zero is the smaller number.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(-52\%<-\frac{10}{20}<-0.495\).

blocks.html: When negative values are close, use the number line to check that the larger distance from zero lies further left.

sections.title: How do I compare close values without losing an exact result?
sections.label: Exact cut-offs
sections.intro: Choose a positive common denominator when one decimal would need rounding. Keep comparison steps exact.

blocks.html: Convert a percentage to hundredths and match denominators if needed. If a limit is ‘at least’, the boundary value qualifies.

blocks.title: Check a cut-off across different forms
blocks.prompt:
A battery indicator passes if it shows at least \(46\%\) of full charge. Which indicators pass?

A \(\frac{47}{100}\); B \(46\%\); C \(0.457\).
blocks.hint: Write all three readings as proportions of full charge and include equality.
blocks.solution:
The decimal cut-off is \(0.460\). ‘At least’ includes equality.

Use the same form: A \(0.470\), B \(0.460\), C \(0.457\).

glossary.definition: Different ways to write the same value.
A whole number and a proper fraction written together.
Two original quantities at exactly the same position.
The value at which a comparison changes.
A comparison that retains the full values and avoids rounding.

revision.body:
Exact equivalent values

If all values give exact terminating decimals, use decimals for the working. A tie stays a tie when the forms change. Write an equals sign where two original values match.

Mixed numbers and negatives

Retain the whole part when rewriting a positive mixed number. Compare signed values by position, and check the requested direction before writing your answer.

Exact cut-offs

Convert a percentage to hundredths and match denominators if needed. If a limit is ‘at least’, the boundary value qualifies.

Example

\(\frac{11}{20}=55\%<0.553\)

Check yourself

  • In increasing order, how do \(\frac25\), \(40\%\) and \(0.407\) compare?
  • Which is larger, \(\frac{5}{12}\) or \(41\%\)?

Answers \(\frac25=40\%<0.407\). \(\frac{5}{12}=\frac{125}{300}>\frac{123}{300}=41\%\).
revision.checks:
• Keep every original entry. Equal numbers can sit next to each other in either order when the list shows equality.
  • A percent above 100% is greater than one. A minus sign changes the position, not just the label.
  • Rounding two different numbers to the same value can create an apparent tie.
revision.examTip: When working without a calculator, compare integer numerators after matching denominators.
